title: Python for Robotics

mentor.name: SERPENT-3
mentor.character: Writes every line as if a two hundred kilo arm were about to run it, and makes you say out loud what the code does before you press run.

summary: You go from your first line of Python to a working two dimensional robot simulator that drives, senses obstacles, follows waypoints and logs its own run. On the way you learn the exact Python a real robot needs: control flow, data structures, files, classes, exceptions, numpy vectors, serial ports and timed control loops.

lessons.title: The First Line of Telemetry
lessons.goal: Print text from a Python program and read the console as a robot's voice.
lessons.theory:
A robot that cannot talk is a robot you cannot debug. On a Raspberry Pi 4 driving a differential base, the very first thing the software does at boot is print a line saying who it is and that it is alive. That line is your only proof the program reached the start.

`print()` writes text to standard output. Everything between the quotes is a **string**, a piece of text. The parentheses are how you call a function: you give it something, it does something with it.

In a real robot this same output ends up in a log file, in a terminal over SSH, or in a service journal. Learning to print clean, boring, informative lines is not a beginner toy, it is the habit that saves you at three in the morning when the arm stops moving and nobody knows why.
lessons.task: The banner already prints. Add a second line so the robot also reports its firmware version, exactly as the solution shows.
lessons.starter: print("ORBITAL-1 booting")
lessons.solution:
print("ORBITAL-1 booting")
print("firmware 0.1.0")
lessons.hint: A second `print()` call on its own line gives you a second line of output.

lessons.title: Naming the Parts
lessons.goal: Store values in variables and reuse them instead of repeating literals.
lessons.theory:
A **variable** is a name attached to a value. You write `wheel_radius = 0.033` and from then on the name `wheel_radius` means 0.033 metres, the radius of the yellow wheels that come with a TT gearmotor.

Why bother? Because a robot has one truth per quantity. If the wheel radius appears as a raw number in nine places and you swap the wheels, you will fix eight of them and spend a weekend hunting the ninth. One name, one place to change.

Python names use lowercase with underscores: `wheel_radius`, `battery_volts`, `left_ticks`. No spaces, no starting with a digit. The `=` sign is not equality, it is assignment: take the value on the right, attach the name on the left.
lessons.task: Create variables for the robot name, the wheel radius in metres and the battery voltage, then print each one.
lessons.starter:
robot_name = "ORBITAL-1"
print(robot_name)
lessons.solution:
robot_name = "ORBITAL-1"
wheel_radius = 0.033
battery_volts = 11.7

print(robot_name)
print(wheel_radius)
print(battery_volts)
lessons.hint: Three assignments first, three `print()` calls after. Do not put quotes around numbers.

lessons.title: Numbers That Move Metal
lessons.goal: Use int and float arithmetic to compute a physical quantity from robot dimensions.
lessons.theory:
Python has two number types you will use constantly. An **int** is a whole number, like the 20 encoder ticks per revolution of a quadrature encoder. A **float** has a decimal point, like 0.033 metres of wheel radius. Divide two ints with `/` and you get a float back, always.

The operators are `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` for normal division, `//` for floor division which throws away the remainder, `%` for the remainder itself, and `**` for powers. Floor division and remainder matter more than you think in robotics: `ticks % ticks_per_rev` tells you where inside a turn the wheel is.

Here is a real calculation. The distance a wheel covers in one full turn is its circumference, `2 * pi * r`. For a 33 millimetre radius wheel that is about 0.207 metres per revolution. Everything a dead reckoning system knows about where the robot is starts from that number.
lessons.task: Compute the wheel circumference from the radius, then `metres_per_tick`, the distance travelled in one encoder tick given 20 ticks per revolution. Print both.
lessons.starter:
PI = 3.14159
wheel_radius = 0.033
ticks_per_rev = 20

circumference = 0.0
print(circumference)
lessons.solution:
PI = 3.14159
wheel_radius = 0.033
ticks_per_rev = 20

circumference = 2 * PI * wheel_radius
metres_per_tick = circumference / ticks_per_rev

print(circumference)
print(metres_per_tick)
lessons.hint: Circumference is `2 * PI * wheel_radius`. One tick covers that divided by the ticks in a revolution.

lessons.title: The Shape of a Status Line
lessons.goal: Build formatted telemetry strings with f-strings and rounding.
lessons.theory:
Raw floats are unreadable. `0.20734493999999998` is not a status line, it is noise. An **f-string** lets you drop values inside text: put an `f` before the quotes and wrap any expression in curly braces.

```
print(f"battery {volts} V")
```

You can also say how it should look. `{volts:.2f}` prints the float with exactly two decimals. `{name:>8}` pads to eight characters on the right. For telemetry, fix your decimals: a battery reading with fourteen digits hides the one digit you care about.

String concatenation with `+` also exists but it forces you to convert numbers by hand with `str()`. Use f-strings. They are shorter, faster and they do not blow up when a value turns out to be a number.
lessons.task: Print one status line with the robot name, the battery voltage to two decimals and the distance per tick to four decimals.
lessons.starter:
robot_name = "ORBITAL-1"
battery_volts = 11.7
metres_per_tick = 0.010367

print(robot_name)
lessons.solution:
robot_name = "ORBITAL-1"
battery_volts = 11.7
metres_per_tick = 0.010367

print(f"{robot_name} | battery {battery_volts:.2f} V | {metres_per_tick:.4f} m/tick")
lessons.hint: One `print(f"...")` with three braces inside. Format specifiers go after a colon, like `:.2f`.

lessons.title: True, False and the Bumper Switch
lessons.goal: Produce boolean values with comparison operators and read them as robot conditions.
lessons.theory:
A bumper switch has exactly two states, pressed or not pressed. Python calls those `True` and `False`, the **bool** type. Capital letters, no quotes: `True` is a value, `"True"` is a piece of text and they are not the same thing.

You rarely type `True` by hand. You produce it by comparing: `distance_cm < 20` is `True` when the HC-SR04 sees something close. The comparison operators are `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==` for equal and `!=` for not equal. Note the double equals: one equals assigns, two compare. Confusing them is the classic first bug.

Every safety decision in a robot bottoms out in a bool. Is the battery below cutoff. Is the arm past its limit. Is the estop pressed. Get comfortable producing these values before you learn to branch on them.
lessons.task: Compute three booleans from the sensor values given: `obstacle_close` under 20 cm, `battery_low` under 10.5 V, and `path_clear` meaning 20 cm or more. Print them in one formatted line.
lessons.starter:
distance_cm = 14.2
battery_volts = 11.7

obstacle_close = False
print(obstacle_close)
lessons.solution:
distance_cm = 14.2
battery_volts = 11.7

obstacle_close = distance_cm < 20
battery_low = battery_volts < 10.5
path_clear = distance_cm >= 20

print(f"close={obstacle_close} low={battery_low} clear={path_clear}")
lessons.hint: Assign the result of a comparison straight into the variable, no `if` needed yet.

lessons.title: The Line You Do Not Cross
lessons.goal: Guard an action with a single if statement and correct indentation.
lessons.theory:
An `if` runs a block of code only when a condition is `True`. The condition goes after the keyword, the line ends with a colon, and the body is **indented four spaces**. In Python indentation is not decoration, it is the syntax. A line that is not indented is not inside the `if`.

This is the shape of every safety guard in a robot. The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor reports a distance in centimetres. Below a threshold you stop the motors. The threshold is not a magic number sprinkled in the code, it is a named constant at the top so the person tuning the robot can find it.

Watch what happens when the condition is `False`: nothing. The block is skipped, the program continues on the next unindented line. A guard that does nothing most of the time is exactly what you want.
lessons.task: Print a stop warning only when the measured distance is below the safety threshold, then print the always running end of cycle line.
lessons.starter:
STOP_CM = 20
distance_cm = 14.2

print("cycle done")
lessons.solution:
STOP_CM = 20
distance_cm = 14.2

if distance_cm < STOP_CM:
    print(f"STOP obstacle at {distance_cm:.1f} cm")

print("cycle done")
lessons.hint: The colon ends the `if` line and the next line is indented four spaces. The final print stays at the left margin.

lessons.title: Two Roads for One Motor
lessons.goal: Choose between two actions with if and else.
lessons.theory:
`else` covers everything the `if` did not. It has no condition of its own, just a colon and an indented block. Exactly one of the two branches runs, never both, never neither.

In a robot this maps onto the most common decision there is: drive or stop. You compute a motor command in one branch and a different one in the other, and after the `if` block the rest of the program uses the value without caring which branch produced it. That pattern, decide then act on one variable, keeps motor writes in a single place, which is where they belong when a bug means a machine moving.

Notice the shape: `motor_pwm` is set in both branches, so after the block it always has a value. If you only set it in one branch, the other path leaves you with a name that does not exist and the program crashes with a NameError.
lessons.task: Set `motor_pwm` to 0 when the obstacle is closer than the threshold and to the cruise value otherwise, then print the command and the distance in one line.
lessons.starter:
STOP_CM = 20
CRUISE_PWM = 160
distance_cm = 42.0

print(f"d={distance_cm:.1f} cm")
lessons.solution:
STOP_CM = 20
CRUISE_PWM = 160
distance_cm = 42.0

if distance_cm < STOP_CM:
    motor_pwm = 0
else:
    motor_pwm = CRUISE_PWM

print(f"d={distance_cm:.1f} cm pwm={motor_pwm}")
lessons.hint: `else:` sits at the same indentation as `if`, with its own indented body.

lessons.title: Three Bands of Distance
lessons.goal: Split a continuous sensor reading into ordered bands with elif.
lessons.theory:
Real robots do not have two speeds, they have a ramp. Far away, drive at cruise. Getting closer, slow down. Too close, stop. That is three cases and `elif` is how you write them.

Python checks the conditions **in order** and stops at the first one that is `True`. That means order is part of the logic. If you test `distance_cm < SLOW_CM` before `distance_cm < STOP_CM`, everything close also matches the first test and the stop band never runs. Write the bands from the tightest to the loosest.

The two thresholds sit at the top of the file in capitals, `STOP_CM` and `SLOW_CM`, because a distance buried as a bare number inside a condition is a number nobody dares touch six months later. Read them by name in the conditions.

An `else` at the end catches whatever is left. With bands ordered from tight to loose, the final `else` is the far case, and it needs no condition at all.
lessons.task: Using the same distance variable and the two thresholds already declared, set the motor command in three bands: stop under `STOP_CM`, slow under `SLOW_CM`, cruise otherwise, and print which band you landed in.
lessons.starter:
STOP_CM = 20
SLOW_CM = 60
distance_cm = 45.0
band = "cruise"
pwm = 160

print(f"{band} {pwm}")
lessons.solution:
STOP_CM = 20
SLOW_CM = 60
SLOW_PWM = 90
CRUISE_PWM = 160
distance_cm = 45.0

if distance_cm < STOP_CM:
    band = "stop"
    pwm = 0
elif distance_cm < SLOW_CM:
    band = "slow"
    pwm = SLOW_PWM
else:
    band = "cruise"
    pwm = CRUISE_PWM

print(f"d={distance_cm:.1f} band={band} pwm={pwm}")
lessons.hint: Tightest threshold first. The `elif` line only runs when the `if` above it was False.

lessons.title: Both Bumpers at Once
lessons.goal: Combine conditions with and, or and not.
lessons.theory:
One sensor is never enough. A small rover carries two lever microswitches on the front bumper, left and right, and the decision depends on both.

`and` is `True` only when both sides are `True`. `or` is `True` when at least one is. `not` flips a bool. They read like English on purpose: `if battery_ok and not estop_pressed:`.

Two details that bite beginners. First, `and` binds tighter than `or`, so `a or b and c` means `a or (b and c)`. When in doubt add parentheses, they cost nothing and they document your intent. Second, Python short circuits: in `a and b`, if `a` is `False` it never even looks at `b`. That is useful when the second check is expensive, like polling a sensor over I2C.
lessons.task: Decide the reverse manoeuvre: set `reverse` when either bumper is pressed, and set `can_drive` only when no bumper is pressed and the estop is not engaged. Print both decisions.
lessons.starter:
bumper_left = True
bumper_right = False
estop = False

reverse = False
print(reverse)
lessons.solution:
bumper_left = True
bumper_right = False
estop = False

reverse = bumper_left or bumper_right
can_drive = not reverse and not estop

if reverse:
    print("reversing, bumper hit")

print(f"reverse={reverse} can_drive={can_drive}")
lessons.hint: `or` for either bumper, then `not` twice for the drive permission.

lessons.title: The Check Inside the Check
lessons.goal: Nest conditions so a decision only happens once its precondition holds.
lessons.theory:
Some decisions only make sense after another one passed. There is no point choosing a driving speed if the battery is already below cutoff: the answer is stop, whatever the ultrasonic says.

You express that by putting an `if` inside another `if`. The inner block is indented eight spaces, two levels. The outer condition is the precondition, the inner one is the detail.

Nesting is powerful and it goes bad fast. Three or four levels deep and nobody can read the code, including you next month. The cure is to flip the precondition into an early exit, which is the next lesson. For now build the nest so you can feel why it gets heavy.

lessons.title: Refusing Early
lessons.goal: Replace nesting with guard clauses that handle the bad case first.
lessons.theory:
A **guard clause** deals with the impossible case immediately and gets out of the way, leaving the rest of the code flat and readable. In a function you would `return`, and you will do exactly that in chapter three. Here you do the same with a status variable and a chain of `elif` bands.

The rule of thumb for robot code: refuse first, act last. List every reason the robot must not move, in priority order, before you compute anything about how it should move. Estop, then a battery under `CUTOFF_V`, then a stale sensor timestamp, then an obstacle inside `STOP_CM`. That ordering is a safety specification written as code, and reading it top to bottom tells a reviewer exactly what wins over what.

Compare this version with the nested one from the previous lesson. Same behaviour, one level of indentation, and adding a fifth refusal reason is a two line change instead of another nest.
lessons.task: Rewrite the same decision as a flat priority chain: estop, then a battery at or below `CUTOFF_V`, then an obstacle closer than `STOP_CM`, then cruise. lessons.title: Inside the Servo Envelope
lessons.goal: Range check a value with a chained comparison and clamp it.
lessons.theory:
An MG996R servo accepts angles from 0 to 180 degrees. Command 200 and you push it against its mechanical stop, it stalls, it draws two amps and it cooks. Every command that leaves your code must be inside the envelope of the hardware that receives it.

Python lets you write a range test the way maths does: `if 0 <= angle <= 180:` is a real, legal chained comparison and it means both halves at once. It is clearer than `angle >= 0 and angle <= 180` and it evaluates `angle` only once.

The partner of the range check is the **clamp**: instead of rejecting an out of range value, you pull it back to the nearest legal one. `min(180, max(0, angle))` reads as, never below 0, never above 180. Clamping is what you want on a live command, rejecting is what you want when validating a config file.
lessons.task: Given a requested angle, report whether it is inside the envelope with a chained comparison and print the clamped value that you would actually send.
lessons.starter:
MIN_DEG = 0
MAX_DEG = 180
requested = 205.0

safe = requested
print(safe)
lessons.solution:
MIN_DEG = 0
MAX_DEG = 180
requested = 205.0

if MIN_DEG <= requested <= MAX_DEG:
    print("request inside envelope")
else:
    print("request out of envelope, clamping")

safe = min(MAX_DEG, max(MIN_DEG, requested))
print(f"requested={requested:.1f} sent={safe:.1f}")
lessons.hint: Write the chained test as `MIN_DEG <= requested <= MAX_DEG`, and clamp with `min` around `max`.

lessons.title: The One Line Verdict
lessons.goal: Write a conditional expression to pick a value inline.
lessons.theory:
Sometimes a four line `if` and `else` exists only to give a variable one of two values. Python has a shorter form for exactly that case, the **conditional expression**:

```
led = "red" if fault else "green"
```

It reads value, condition, other value. It is an expression, so it can go anywhere a value goes: inside an f-string, as a function argument, inside a list.

Use it when both outcomes are simple values. The moment a branch needs two statements, go back to the block form. Cramming logic into one line is not skill, it is a debt you pay when the robot misbehaves and you cannot set a breakpoint inside a line.
lessons.task: Rebuild the priority chain result as a single flag called `blocked`, true when the estop is pressed or the way is too close, then build the status LED colour and the direction word with conditional expressions and print a single status line. The colour is `red` when `blocked` holds and `green` when it does not, and the direction word is `hold` against `forward`.
lessons.starter:
estop = False
distance_cm = 12.0
STOP_CM = 20

led = "green"
print(led)
lessons.solution:
STOP_CM = 20
estop = False
distance_cm = 12.0

blocked = estop or distance_cm < STOP_CM
led = "red" if blocked else "green"
direction = "hold" if blocked else "forward"

print(f"led={led} direction={direction} d={distance_cm:.1f}")
lessons.hint: The shape is `value_if_true if condition else value_if_false`, all on one line.

lessons.title: Ten Pings and Stop
lessons.goal: Repeat a block a fixed number of times with a while loop and a counter.
lessons.theory:
A `while` loop repeats its body as long as a condition stays `True`. Three parts have to be there or the loop misbehaves: initialise the counter before the loop, test it in the condition, and change it inside the body. Forget the third and the condition never becomes `False`, which is an infinite loop.

Why count samples at all? Because an HC-SR04 is noisy. A single ping can come back wrong if the echo bounced off a table edge. Robotics code almost never trusts one reading, it takes a burst and works on the burst.

The body is indented like an `if` body. The condition is checked before every pass, so a loop whose condition starts out `False` runs zero times, which is a legitimate and useful outcome.
lessons.task: Take ten simulated pings by looping a counter from 0 to 9 and printing the sample index and a distance that grows 1.5 cm each pass.
lessons.starter:
SAMPLES = 10
i = 0
distance_cm = 20.0

print(f"sample {i} d={distance_cm:.1f}")
lessons.solution:
SAMPLES = 10
i = 0
distance_cm = 20.0

while i < SAMPLES:
    print(f"sample {i} d={distance_cm:.1f}")
    distance_cm = distance_cm + 1.5
    i = i + 1

print("burst complete")
lessons.hint: The counter increment `i = i + 1` goes inside the loop body, as the last line.

lessons.title: Sweeping the Servo
lessons.goal: Iterate over a numeric sequence with for and range.
lessons.theory:
When you know how many times you want to repeat, `for` with `range()` says it in one line and cannot forget the increment. `for angle in range(0, 181, 10):` walks 0, 10, 20 and so on up to 180.

`range(stop)` starts at 0. `range(start, stop)` starts where you say. `range(start, stop, step)` adds the step. The **stop value is never included**, which is why a sweep to 180 has to say 181. That off by one is not a Python quirk to memorise, it is the same convention that makes `range(n)` give exactly `n` values.

This is the classic pan servo sweep: an SG90 on a bracket, an ultrasonic sensor on top, one reading per step. The loop variable is the commanded angle and you use it directly in the body.
lessons.task: Sweep from 0 to 180 degrees in steps of 15 and print each commanded angle, then print how many positions the sweep visited.
lessons.starter:
for angle in range(0, 31, 15):
    print(f"servo -> {angle} deg")
lessons.solution:
STEP_DEG = 15
positions = 0

for angle in range(0, 181, STEP_DEG):
    print(f"servo -> {angle} deg")
    positions = positions + 1

print(f"sweep visited {positions} positions")
lessons.hint: `range(0, 181, STEP_DEG)` includes 180 because the stop bound is exclusive.

lessons.title: The Return Sweep
lessons.goal: Walk a range backwards with a negative step.
lessons.theory:
A pan servo that only sweeps one way has to snap back to zero, which shakes the whole chassis and ruins the next reading. Real sweeps go out and come back, and the return leg is a `range` with a negative step.

`range(180, -1, -15)` starts at 180, decreases by 15 and stops before -1, so it ends exactly at 0. The exclusive stop bound works the same way going down, which is why the stop is -1 and not 0.

A negative step with a start below the stop produces an empty range and the loop simply never runs. Python will not warn you. If a loop mysteriously does nothing, check the direction of your step first.
lessons.task: Do a full out and back sweep: 0 to 180 in steps of 15, then 180 back down to 0 in the same step, printing the direction and the angle.
lessons.hint: The return leg is `range(180, -1, -STEP_DEG)`, stop is one past the last value you want.

lessons.title: The Average of the Burst
lessons.goal: Accumulate a running total inside a loop and divide to get a mean.
lessons.theory:
An **accumulator** is a variable declared before the loop and added to inside it. Total starts at zero, each pass adds a reading, after the loop you divide by the count and you have the mean.

This is the cheapest filter in robotics and it buys a lot. An MPU6050 accelerometer at rest reports values wobbling by a few hundredths of a g from sample to sample. Average sixteen of them and the wobble drops noticeably, at the cost of the delay those sixteen samples took.

Declare the accumulator outside the loop. Put it inside and it resets on every pass, which gives you the last reading instead of the mean, and it looks almost right, which is the worst kind of bug.
lessons.task: Simulate a burst of eight readings that drift upward, accumulate the total inside the loop, and print the mean at the end.
lessons.starter:
SAMPLES = 8
total = 0.0
reading = 21.0

print(total)
lessons.solution:
SAMPLES = 8
total = 0.0
reading = 21.0

for i in range(SAMPLES):
    print(f"sample {i} d={reading:.2f}")
    total = total + reading
    reading = reading + 0.4

mean = total / SAMPLES
print(f"mean distance {mean:.2f} cm over {SAMPLES} samples")
lessons.hint: `total = total + reading` inside the loop, the division by `SAMPLES` after it.

lessons.title: Stop the Scan on Contact
lessons.goal: Leave a loop early with break when the answer is already known.
lessons.theory:
`break` ends the loop immediately. The rest of the body is skipped and execution continues after the loop.

A scanning robot does not need to finish its sweep once it has found what it was looking for. If the sensor sees a wall at 12 cm on the third of twelve positions, the remaining nine readings cost time the robot does not have. Break out, act on the bearing you found.

Record what you found before you break. A common mistake is to break and then discover that the loop variable is not what you assumed, or that no variable outside the loop holds the result. Store the bearing in a variable declared before the loop, set it, then break.
lessons.task: Sweep in steps of 20 degrees through a list of simulated readings, and break as soon as a reading is under the alarm threshold, saving the bearing where it happened.
lessons.solution:
ALARM_CM = 25
readings = [80.0, 62.0, 18.0, 40.0, 55.0, 70.0, 90.0, 95.0, 88.0, 75.0]
hit_bearing = -1

for i in range(len(readings)):
    bearing = i * 20
    d = readings[i]
    print(f"bearing {bearing:3d} deg d={d:.1f}")
    if d < ALARM_CM:
        hit_bearing = bearing
        break

if hit_bearing >= 0:
    print(f"obstacle found at {hit_bearing} deg, scan aborted")
else:
    print("sector clear")
lessons.hint: Set `hit_bearing` on the line before `break`, otherwise the information dies with the loop.

lessons.title: Throwing Away the Bad Ping
lessons.goal: Skip one pass of a loop with continue to filter invalid readings.
lessons.theory:
`continue` jumps straight to the next pass. Everything below it in the body is skipped, but the loop keeps going.

This is how you drop garbage sensor data. An HC-SR04 returns 0 when the echo never came back, and anything above `MAX_CM`, its four metre ceiling, is beyond its usable range. Those two values are not measurements, they are failures, and averaging them into your distance estimate poisons it. Detect them at the top of the body and `continue`.

Count what you dropped. A loop that silently discards half its input while the robot keeps driving is worse than one that fails loudly. Keep a `rejected` counter and print it, so a sensor going bad shows up as a rising rejection rate instead of a mystery.
lessons.task: Loop over the raw readings with `for d in raw:`, skip the zeros and anything over `MAX_CM` with `continue`, count the accepted and rejected samples and print the mean of the accepted ones.
lessons.solution:
MAX_CM = 400.0
raw = [42.0, 0.0, 39.5, 512.0, 41.0, 0.0, 40.5, 38.0]
accepted = 0
rejected = 0
total = 0.0

for d in raw:
    if d <= 0.0 or d > MAX_CM:
        rejected = rejected + 1
        continue
    total = total + d
    accepted = accepted + 1

mean = total / accepted
print(f"accepted={accepted} rejected={rejected} mean={mean:.2f} cm")
lessons.hint: The `continue` goes right after you count the rejection, before any accumulation.

lessons.title: The Pan and Tilt Grid
lessons.goal: Nest one loop inside another to cover a two axis scan.
lessons.theory:
A pan and tilt head has two servos, so covering the field means two loops, one inside the other. The outer loop moves the slow axis, tilt, and the inner loop sweeps the fast one, pan. For every single tilt position, the whole pan sweep runs.

That multiplication is the thing to internalise: 5 tilt steps by 13 pan steps is 65 measurements, and at 60 milliseconds per ultrasonic ping that is about four seconds of scanning. Nested loops are where robot code quietly becomes too slow, and the fix is always to reduce one of the two ranges, not to make the body faster.

The inner loop variable is fresh on every outer pass. The outer variable is visible inside the inner body, which is exactly how you build a coordinate pair from the two.
lessons.task: Scan a grid: tilt from -20 to 20 in steps of 20, and for each tilt sweep pan from 0 to 180 in steps of 60. Count the total measurements and print each cell.
lessons.starter:
for tilt in range(-20, 21, 20):
    print(f"tilt {tilt}")
lessons.hint: The inner `for` is indented inside the outer body, and its own body is indented one level further. Start a counter called `cells` at zero before the outer loop and add one to it in the innermost body.

lessons.title: The Loop That Never Ends
lessons.goal: Structure a control loop as while True with explicit exit conditions.
lessons.theory:
Robot software is one big loop: read sensors, decide, write actuators, repeat, forever. You write that as `while True:` and it is the correct shape, not a beginner shortcut. Every ROS node, every Arduino sketch, every flight controller is this loop.

Since the condition is always `True`, the exits are all explicit `break` statements inside the body, one per reason to stop: the mission finished, the estop fired, the battery hit cutoff, an iteration cap was reached. Naming each exit is what makes the loop safe to reason about.

Always include a hard iteration cap while you are developing, `MAX_TICKS` here, and a goal distance you can read by name, `GOAL_M`. A control loop that will not exit and drives motors is how a robot walks off a bench. The cap is a seatbelt you remove only when the other exits are proven.
lessons.task: Write the control loop with three exits: mission complete when the travelled distance passes `GOAL_M`, an estop check, and a hard cap of `MAX_TICKS` iterations. Set `reason` to "goal reached", "estop" or "iteration cap" before each `break`, and print it.
lessons.starter:
GOAL_M = 2.0
MAX_TICKS = 200
travelled_m = 0.0
ticks = 0
reason = "none"

print(reason)
lessons.solution:
GOAL_M = 2.0
MAX_TICKS = 200
STEP_M = 0.05
travelled_m = 0.0
ticks = 0
estop = False
reason = "none"

while True:
    ticks = ticks + 1
    travelled_m = travelled_m + STEP_M

    if estop:
        reason = "estop"
        break
    if travelled_m >= GOAL_M:
        reason = "goal reached"
        break
    if ticks >= MAX_TICKS:
        reason = "iteration cap"
        break

print(f"stopped after {ticks} ticks, {travelled_m:.2f} m, reason: {reason}")
lessons.hint: `while True:` with three separate `if` blocks inside, each setting `reason` before its `break`.

lessons.title: The Closest Thing Out There
lessons.goal: Track a running minimum through a loop to find the nearest obstacle.
lessons.theory:
Finding the smallest value in a stream is a loop pattern worth knowing cold. Keep two variables outside the loop: the best value so far and where it happened. On each pass, if the current reading beats the best, replace both.

Initialise the best to something that any real reading beats. For a minimum distance, a very large number like 9999.0 works, and it also serves as a sentinel: if it survives the loop unchanged, nothing valid was seen at all.

This is the core of obstacle avoidance. A 360 degree lidar hands you hundreds of ranges and the only question the avoidance behaviour asks is, what is the closest return and in which direction. Everything else is filtering.
lessons.task: Scan the readings, skip the invalid zeros, and track both the smallest valid distance and the bearing where it was measured, at 30 degrees per index. Print the result or report an empty scan.
lessons.hint: Update `nearest_cm` and `nearest_deg` together inside the same `if`, never separately.

lessons.title: Sealing a Behaviour in a Box
lessons.goal: Define a function with def and call it by name.
lessons.theory:
A **function** is a block of code with a name. You write it once with `def`, and from then on you run it by writing its name followed by parentheses. Defining it does nothing on its own, the body only runs when you call it.

The first reason to make one is not reuse, it is naming. `emergency_stop()` tells a reader what those four lines do without them reading the four lines. Robot code is full of sequences that have an obvious name and a non obvious body: park the arm, kill the drivers, flush the log.

The body is indented under the `def` line, same rule as `if` and `for`. Define the function before you call it, because Python reads the file top to bottom and cannot call a name it has not seen yet.
lessons.task: The stop sequence runs inline below. Move it into a function called `emergency_stop` and then call it twice, to prove that defining and running are different things.
lessons.starter:
print("ready")
print("motors to zero")
print("brakes engaged")
print("driver power cut")

# TODO: move the stop sequence into a function, then run it twice
lessons.solution:
def emergency_stop():
    print("motors to zero")
    print("brakes engaged")
    print("driver power cut")

print("ready")
emergency_stop()
emergency_stop()
lessons.hint: The `def` block only defines. Add a line with `emergency_stop()` at the left margin to actually run it.

lessons.title: Feeding the Box
lessons.goal: Pass arguments into a function through parameters.
lessons.theory:
A function that always does the same thing is a paragraph with a title. A function that takes **parameters** is a tool. The names in the `def` line are the parameters, the values you pass at the call are the arguments, and inside the body the parameters behave like ordinary variables.

Unit conversion is the perfect first case, and it is not busywork. Encoders count ticks, motion planners want metres, and the two must never meet without a conversion in between. Writing it once as `ticks_to_metres(ticks)` means the wheel radius appears in exactly one place in the codebase.

Parameters are matched by position by default: the first argument fills the first parameter. Swap two arguments of the same type and Python will not complain, it will just give you a wrong number, which is why the next lessons push you toward names.
lessons.task: Write `ticks_to_metres(ticks)` using the module level constants, and call it with 20, 100 and 137 ticks, printing each conversion.
lessons.starter:
PI = 3.14159
WHEEL_R = 0.033
TICKS_PER_REV = 20

def ticks_to_metres(ticks):
    return 0.0

print(ticks_to_metres(20))
lessons.solution:
PI = 3.14159
WHEEL_R = 0.033
TICKS_PER_REV = 20

def ticks_to_metres(ticks):
    circumference = 2 * PI * WHEEL_R
    return ticks / TICKS_PER_REV * circumference

for t in (20, 100, 137):
    print(f"{t:4d} ticks = {ticks_to_metres(t):.4f} m")
lessons.hint: The parameter `ticks` is used inside the body exactly like a variable you assigned.

lessons.title: Handing Back the Answer
lessons.goal: Return a value from a function and use it in an expression.
lessons.theory:
`return` sends a value back to whoever called the function and ends the function immediately. Without a `return`, a function hands back `None`, which is Python's way of saying nothing. A function that prints instead of returning is a dead end: you cannot use its result in another calculation.

The rule that will serve you for years: **compute and return, do not print inside**. A `clamp` that prints the clamped value is useless inside a control loop running at 100 Hz. A `clamp` that returns it can be composed with anything.

A function can have several `return` statements. The first one that runs wins, the rest never execute. That is what makes guard clauses work: refuse early, return early, and the happy path stays flat at the bottom.
lessons.task: Write `clamp(value, low, high)` that returns the value pulled into range, using early returns, and use it to sanitise three motor commands.
lessons.hint: Three `return` statements, no `else` needed. The last one is the value that was already in range.

lessons.title: Sensible Defaults
lessons.goal: Give parameters default values so common calls stay short.
lessons.theory:
A parameter with a default becomes optional: `def drive(speed, ramp=0.2):` can be called as `drive(0.4)` or as `drive(0.4, ramp=0.05)`. Defaults are written in the `def` line and they must come after all the parameters that have none.

Defaults encode the sane configuration of your robot. The acceleration ramp that keeps the wheels from slipping, the timeout that matches your sensor rate, the PWM ceiling your driver survives. Someone calling your function gets those for free and only overrides what their situation actually needs.

One trap that costs people hours: never use a mutable object like a list as a default value. That default is created once, when the function is defined, and it is shared by every call. You will meet lists in the next chapter, so file this away now.
lessons.task: Write `motor_command(speed, limit=255, deadband=15)` that clamps to the limit and forces small commands to zero, then call it with and without overrides, including one call that lowers the ceiling with `limit=180` for a driver that cannot take the full range.
lessons.hint: Defaults go in the `def` line as `limit=255`, and an override at the call site is written the same way. Clamp the speed into a local called `cmd` first, then test `cmd` against the deadband before you return it.

lessons.title: Two Numbers, One Return
lessons.goal: Return several values at once as a tuple and unpack them at the call site.
lessons.theory:
`return x, y` hands back a **tuple**, an immutable little package of values. At the call site you unpack it with `x, y = odometry_step(...)` and the two names land in one line.

Robotics is full of naturally paired values. A pose is x, y and heading. A differential drive command is left and right wheel speed. A calibration is offset and scale. Splitting those into separate functions means computing the same intermediate twice, which is both slower and a chance for the two halves to drift apart.

Unpacking is strict: the number of names on the left must match the number of values in the tuple. If you only want part of it, you can index it like `result[0]`, but naming both is clearer. Use `_` as a name for a value you deliberately ignore.
lessons.task: Write `wheel_speeds(v, omega)` that converts a linear and angular command into the left and right wheel speeds `v_left` and `v_right` for a 0.16 m wheelbase, and unpack the result.
lessons.starter:
WHEELBASE_M = 0.16

def wheel_speeds(v, omega):
    return 0.0, 0.0

left, right = wheel_speeds(0.3, 0.5)
print(left, right)
lessons.solution:
WHEELBASE_M = 0.16

def wheel_speeds(v, omega):
    half = WHEELBASE_M / 2.0
    v_left = v - omega * half
    v_right = v + omega * half
    return v_left, v_right

left, right = wheel_speeds(0.3, 0.5)
print(f"v=0.30 w=0.50 -> left {left:.3f} m/s right {right:.3f} m/s")

left, right = wheel_speeds(0.0, 1.2)
print(f"spin in place -> left {left:.3f} m/s right {right:.3f} m/s")
lessons.hint: Return the two speeds separated by a comma, and unpack with two names separated by a comma.

lessons.title: What Happens in the Function
lessons.goal: Understand local scope and why shared mutable state hurts robot code.
lessons.theory:
A name created inside a function is **local**: it exists only while the function runs and it is invisible outside. Assigning to it does not touch a variable of the same name at module level, it creates a separate one.

A function can read a module level name it never assigned, which is how constants like `WHEELBASE_M` work. But the moment a function assigns to that name anywhere in its body, Python treats it as local for the whole function, and reading it before the assignment raises an UnboundLocalError. The `global` keyword exists to override this and you should treat it as a smell.

Why this matters at 100 Hz: a function that quietly mutates shared state is impossible to test and impossible to reason about when two behaviours run in the same loop. Take inputs as parameters, hand results back with `return`, and let the caller decide what to store. That habit is what makes the simulator in chapter nine possible to debug.
lessons.task: Prove the rule: write a function that takes the pose as parameters and returns a new pose, and show that a local assignment inside it leaves the module level pose untouched until you reassign it yourself.
lessons.starter:
robot_x = 0.0

def advance(x, step):
    return x

print(robot_x)
lessons.solution:
STEP_M = 0.25
robot_x = 0.0

def advance(x, step):
    x = x + step
    return x

new_x = advance(robot_x, STEP_M)
print(f"inside returned {new_x:.2f}, module level still {robot_x:.2f}")

robot_x = advance(robot_x, STEP_M)
print(f"after reassigning, module level is {robot_x:.2f}")
lessons.hint: The `x = x + step` inside the function touches only the local copy. The caller has to assign the returned value.

lessons.title: Writing Down the Contract
lessons.goal: Document a function with a docstring and type hints.
lessons.theory:
A **docstring** is a string on the first line of the function body, written with triple quotes. Tools read it, editors show it on hover, and `help(fn)` prints it. **Type hints** annotate what goes in and what comes out: `def clamp(value: float, low: float, high: float) -> float:`.

Neither is enforced at runtime. Python will happily pass a string where you hinted a float. That is fine, because the audience is human and static checkers. In robotics the payoff is units: the hint says `float`, the docstring says `metres per second`, and the next person does not feed it centimetres.

Keep the docstring to what a caller needs: what it does, what the arguments mean including units, what it returns, and what it refuses. Do not narrate the implementation, the implementation is right there.
lessons.task: Take the wheel speed function, add type hints and a docstring that states the units of every argument and of the return, then print the docstring.
lessons.starter:
WHEELBASE_M = 0.16

def wheel_speeds(v, omega):
    half = WHEELBASE_M / 2.0
    return v - omega * half, v + omega * half

print(wheel_speeds(0.3, 0.5))
lessons.solution:
WHEELBASE_M = 0.16

def wheel_speeds(v: float, omega: float) -> tuple:
    """Convert a body velocity into differential wheel speeds.

    v: forward velocity in metres per second, positive ahead.
    omega: yaw rate in radians per second, positive counter clockwise.
    Returns (v_left, v_right) in metres per second.
    """
    half = WHEELBASE_M / 2.0
    return v - omega * half, v + omega * half

print(wheel_speeds.__doc__)
print(wheel_speeds(0.3, 0.5))
lessons.hint: The docstring is the very first thing inside the body, wrapped in triple double quotes.

lessons.title: Small Boxes Inside Bigger Boxes
lessons.goal: Compose small functions into one behaviour function.
lessons.theory:
The way real robot software is built: several tiny functions that each do one honest thing, and one function on top that calls them in order. The top one reads like a description of the behaviour and contains almost no arithmetic.

Here you assemble the pieces from this chapter into `avoidance_step(distance_cm, battery_volts)`. It decides a body velocity, converts it to wheel speeds, clamps both, and returns the pair. Each step is already written and already tested.

The test for good decomposition is whether you can change one piece without opening the others. Swap the avoidance rule for a proportional one and `wheel_speeds` never moves. Change the wheelbase and the avoidance rule never moves. That independence is the entire point.
lessons.task: Write `body_command(distance_cm, battery_volts)` that picks the body velocity and yaw rate, then `avoidance_step(distance_cm, battery_volts)` that turns that into clamped left and right wheel speeds with `wheel_speeds` and `clamp`, and print the result for three situations.
lessons.hint: `avoidance_step` should contain three calls and one return, no arithmetic of its own.

lessons.title: Calling Things by Their Name
lessons.goal: Use keyword arguments so a call site says what each value means.
lessons.theory:
`set_pid(0.8, 0.02, 0.1, 255, 0.05)` is a line nobody can review. `set_pid(kp=0.8, ki=0.02, kd=0.1, limit=255, dt=0.05)` is the same call and it needs no comment. That is a **keyword argument**: you name the parameter at the call site.

Keywords can be given in any order and can be mixed with positional arguments, as long as every positional one comes first. In practice: pass the one or two obvious values positionally, name everything else, especially booleans. `home(fast=True)` beats `home(True)` every time.

A function definition can also demand it. Anything after a bare `*` in the parameter list is keyword only, so `def move(distance, *, blocking=False)` makes `move(1.0, True)` a syntax error instead of a silent misunderstanding. On a machine that moves, forcing the caller to be explicit is cheap insurance.
lessons.task: Write `configure_drive` with keyword only options after a bare `*`, one of them `reversed_left` for a mirrored left motor, call it once with defaults and once with three named overrides, printing the resulting configuration line.
lessons.solution:
def configure_drive(name, *, max_speed=0.45, ramp=0.20, reversed_left=False, deadband=15):
    sense = "reversed" if reversed_left else "normal"
    print(f"{name}: max {max_speed:.2f} m/s, ramp {ramp:.2f} s, left {sense}, deadband {deadband}")

configure_drive("ORBITAL-1")
configure_drive("ORBITAL-1", max_speed=0.30, ramp=0.05, reversed_left=True)
lessons.hint: The bare `*` in the parameter list forces every later argument to be passed by name.

lessons.title: A Row of Ranges
lessons.goal: Create a list and read its elements by index.
lessons.theory:
A **list** holds several values in order, written between square brackets and separated by commas. An RPLIDAR A1 hands your program hundreds of ranges per revolution and a list is the natural container for them.

You read an element with `ranges[0]`, and the first index is **zero**. The last element is `ranges[len(ranges) - 1]`, or more simply `ranges[-1]`, because negative indices count backwards from the end. `len()` gives the number of elements, which is one more than the highest valid index.

Asking for an index that does not exist raises an IndexError and stops the program. That is a feature: a lidar scan that came back short should crash your test, not silently return the wrong bearing.
lessons.task: Build the scan list, then print the number of samples, the first, the last with a negative index, and the sample at index 3.
lessons.solution:
ranges_cm = [120.0, 84.5, 33.2, 47.0, 91.0, 150.0, 62.0, 28.7]

print(f"samples: {len(ranges_cm)}")
print(f"first:   {ranges_cm[0]:.1f} cm")
print(f"last:    {ranges_cm[-1]:.1f} cm")
print(f"index 3: {ranges_cm[3]:.1f} cm at {3 * 45} deg")
lessons.hint: `len()` counts, `[0]` is the first, `[-1]` is the last.

lessons.title: The Slice in Front
lessons.goal: Take a sub list with slicing to isolate a sector of a scan.
lessons.theory:
A **slice** copies a range of elements: `ranges[2:5]` gives elements 2, 3 and 4. The start is included, the stop is not, exactly like `range()`. Leave a side blank and it means all the way to that end: `ranges[:4]` is the first four, `ranges[-3:]` is the last three.

This is how you cut a scan into sectors. With 12 samples covering 360 degrees, the forward sector is the samples around index 0, the left sector is the middle third, and each is a slice you can then reduce to a single number. Obstacle avoidance is mostly this: slice, reduce, compare.

A slice always returns a **new list**. Changing the slice does not change the original, which is what you want when a behaviour inspects a scan without being allowed to corrupt it.
lessons.task: Slice the 12 sample scan into three 4 sample sectors, right, front and left, and print each sector with its minimum range.
lessons.solution:
scan = [120.0, 84.5, 33.2, 47.0, 91.0, 150.0, 62.0, 28.7, 44.1, 77.0, 99.0, 110.0]

right = scan[0:4]
front = scan[4:8]
left = scan[8:]

print(f"right {right} min {min(right):.1f}")
print(f"front {front} min {min(front):.1f}")
print(f"left  {left} min {min(left):.1f}")
lessons.hint: `scan[4:8]` takes indices 4 to 7. Leaving the stop out, `scan[8:]`, runs to the end.

lessons.title: The Rolling Buffer
lessons.goal: Grow and shrink a list with append and pop to keep a fixed window.
lessons.theory:
Lists are **mutable**: you can change them after creation. `buffer.append(value)` adds one at the end, `buffer.pop(0)` removes and returns the first, `buffer.pop()` removes the last.

A fixed length rolling buffer is the workhorse of sensor code. Every cycle you append the new reading, and if the buffer grew past its window you pop the oldest. What is left is always the last N samples, which is what a moving average or a spike detector needs.

Watch out: `buffer.append` modifies the list in place and returns `None`. Writing `buffer = buffer.append(x)` destroys your buffer and replaces it with nothing. That mistake is a rite of passage, skip it by remembering that mutating methods on lists return `None`.
lessons.task: Simulate a stream of readings feeding a rolling buffer of length 5, popping the oldest when it overflows, and print the buffer and its mean on every cycle.
lessons.solution:
WINDOW = 5
stream = [21.0, 22.5, 20.0, 23.5, 24.0, 60.0, 25.0, 24.5]
buffer = []

for reading in stream:
    buffer.append(reading)
    if len(buffer) > WINDOW:
        buffer.pop(0)
    mean = sum(buffer) / len(buffer)
    print(f"buffer={buffer} mean={mean:.2f}")
lessons.hint: Append first, then check the length and `pop(0)` if it is too long.

lessons.title: Every Beam Has an Angle
lessons.goal: Iterate a list with for and get the index too using enumerate.
lessons.theory:
`for r in scan:` walks the values and is the clearest way to read a list. But a lidar sample means nothing without its bearing, and the bearing comes from the index.

`enumerate(scan)` hands you both at once: `for i, r in enumerate(scan):` gives the index in `i` and the value in `r`. It is cleaner and faster than `for i in range(len(scan)):` followed by an index lookup, and it never goes out of bounds.

`enumerate` takes a `start` if your hardware numbers beams from 1. Convert the index to a real angle with the angular resolution of the sensor: with 12 beams over 360 degrees that is 30 degrees per index, and that multiplication belongs in one place, not repeated in every behaviour.
lessons.task: Compute `deg_per_beam` from the number of beams, walk the scan with `enumerate`, convert each index to a bearing in degrees, and print only the beams that see something closer than the alarm distance.
lessons.solution:
ALARM_CM = 50.0
scan = [120.0, 84.5, 33.2, 47.0, 91.0, 150.0, 62.0, 28.7, 44.1, 77.0, 99.0, 110.0]
deg_per_beam = 360.0 / len(scan)

for i, r in enumerate(scan):
    bearing = i * deg_per_beam
    if r < ALARM_CM:
        print(f"beam {i:2d} at {bearing:5.1f} deg sees {r:.1f} cm")
lessons.hint: `for i, r in enumerate(scan):` unpacks the index and the value in one line.

lessons.title: Reducing a Scan to a Number
lessons.goal: Summarise a list with len, sum, min and max.
lessons.theory:
Four builtins collapse a whole list into one value: `len` counts, `sum` adds, `min` finds the smallest, `max` the largest. Together they replace the accumulator loops you wrote in chapter two, and they are implemented in C so they are far faster on a Raspberry Pi.

The decision layer of a robot almost never wants a list, it wants a number. What is the closest return in the front sector. What is the mean of the burst. Reduce early, decide on scalars.

`min` and `max` on an empty list raise a ValueError. In a robot that means a scan that arrived empty crashes your behaviour, so either guard with `if scan:` or pass a default, `min(scan, default=999.0)`. Choose deliberately, because both silently wrong and loudly crashed have their place.
lessons.task: Write `summarise(values)` that returns count, minimum, maximum and mean, guarding the empty list case, and print the summary of the front sector.
lessons.starter:
scan = [120.0, 84.5, 33.2, 47.0, 91.0, 150.0, 62.0, 28.7]

def summarise(values):
    return 0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0

print(summarise(scan))
lessons.hint: `if not values:` is the empty guard. Return the four numbers as one tuple.

lessons.title: The Median Beats the Mean
lessons.goal: Sort a list and pick the middle value to reject spikes.
lessons.theory:
`sorted(values)` returns a new sorted list, `values.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. Prefer `sorted` unless you have a reason, for the same reason you prefer returning over mutating.

Sorting buys you the **median**, the middle value of the sorted list. One wild reading, the 512 cm an ultrasonic sensor produces when the echo misses, drags a mean badly and does not move a median at all. For sensors that fail by producing occasional nonsense rather than gentle noise, the median filter is the correct first choice and it is four lines.

With an odd count the median is `s[n // 2]`. With an even count it is the average of the two middle elements. Floor division with `//` is what gets you the index, and this is one of the few places where it appears naturally.
lessons.task: Write `median(values)` handling both odd and even counts, then compare mean and median on a burst that contains one bad spike.
lessons.starter:
burst = [41.0, 40.5, 512.0, 39.8, 41.2]

def median(values):
    return 0.0

print(median(burst))
lessons.solution:
burst = [41.0, 40.5, 512.0, 39.8, 41.2]

def median(values):
    s = sorted(values)
    n = len(s)
    mid = n // 2
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return s[mid]
    return (s[mid - 1] + s[mid]) / 2.0

mean = sum(burst) / len(burst)
print(f"mean   {mean:.2f} cm")
print(f"median {median(burst):.2f} cm")
print(f"even count median {median([39.8, 40.5, 41.0, 41.2]):.2f} cm")
lessons.hint: Sort first, then `n // 2` is the middle index. Check `n % 2` to know which case you are in.

lessons.title: Building a List in One Line
lessons.goal: Transform and filter a list with a comprehension.
lessons.theory:
A **list comprehension** builds a new list from an old one: `[r / 100.0 for r in scan]` converts every centimetre reading to metres. Add a condition and it filters too: `[r for r in scan if r > 0]` drops the invalid zeros.

Read it left to right as an English sentence: the expression to produce, for each element, optionally when a condition holds. It replaces the append loop you wrote by hand, and on a list of a thousand lidar points it is measurably faster.

Keep them to one operation. A comprehension with two conditions, a nested loop and a conditional expression inside is a puzzle, not code. When it stops fitting comfortably on one line, write the loop.
lessons.task: In one comprehension, convert the raw millimetre readings to metres while dropping every invalid zero, then print how many survived and the resulting list.
lessons.solution:
raw_mm = [1204, 0, 845, 332, 0, 470, 910, 1500, 620, 287]

valid_m = [mm / 1000.0 for mm in raw_mm if mm > 0]
near = [d for d in valid_m if d < 0.5]

print(f"{len(valid_m)} of {len(raw_mm)} readings valid")
print([f"{d:.3f}" for d in valid_m])
print(f"{len(near)} returns closer than 0.5 m")
lessons.hint: The shape is `[expression for item in source if condition]`, all inside square brackets.

value: [mm / 1000.0 for mm in raw_mm if mm > 0]

lessons.title: The Grid Under the Wheels
lessons.goal: Represent an occupancy grid as a list of lists and index it by row and column.
lessons.theory:
A map is a two dimensional array, and in plain Python that is a list whose elements are lists. `grid[row][col]` reads one cell: the first index picks the row, the second picks the column inside it.

Build it with a comprehension: `[[0 for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(rows)]` creates independent rows. Do not build it with `[[0] * cols] * rows`, that repeats the **same** row object and writing one cell writes the whole column, a bug that looks like haunted hardware.

Occupancy grids are how a robot remembers what it has seen. 0 for free, 1 for occupied, and a conversion from metres to cell indices using the resolution: `col = int(x_m / RES_M)`. Keep that conversion in one function, because getting it wrong flips your map on the diagonal.
lessons.task: Build a 6 by 8 grid of zeros, mark three obstacle cells given in metres with a `to_cell(x_m, y_m)` conversion, and print the map with one character per cell.
lessons.starter:
ROWS = 6
COLS = 8
RES_M = 0.25

grid = [[0 for _ in range(COLS)] for _ in range(ROWS)]

print(grid[0])
lessons.hint: `grid[row][col] = 1` marks a cell. Build the rows with a nested comprehension so each row is its own list.

lessons.title: Waypoints Are Not Lists
lessons.goal: Use tuples for fixed records and pair sequences with zip.
lessons.theory:
A **tuple** is written with commas, usually inside parentheses, and it cannot be changed after creation. `(1.5, 0.8)` is a waypoint. That immutability is the point: a coordinate pair has exactly two fields forever, and a function that receives it cannot append a third one behind your back.

Unpack a tuple in a `for` header and both fields get names: `for x, y in waypoints:` is far better than `wp[0]` and `wp[1]` scattered through the body.

`zip(a, b)` walks two sequences in step, giving one tuple per position, and it stops at the shorter one. Pairing each waypoint with the next one is the standard way to walk the legs of a path: `zip(path, path[1:])`.
lessons.task: Store a path as a list of tuples, then use `zip` against the shifted path to walk each leg and print its length, accumulating the total path distance in `total_m`.
lessons.solution:
import math

path = [(0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 0.0), (1.0, 0.8), (2.2, 0.8)]
total_m = 0.0

for start, end in zip(path, path[1:]):
    x0, y0 = start
    x1, y1 = end
    leg = math.hypot(x1 - x0, y1 - y0)
    total_m = total_m + leg
    print(f"({x0:.1f},{y0:.1f}) -> ({x1:.1f},{y1:.1f}) leg {leg:.3f} m")

print(f"path length {total_m:.3f} m over {len(path) - 1} legs")
lessons.hint: `zip(path, path[1:])` pairs each waypoint with the following one. Unpack both tuples inside the loop.

lessons.title: The Robot in a Dictionary
lessons.goal: Create a dict and read values by key.
lessons.theory:
A list is indexed by position, a **dict** is indexed by name. You write it with curly braces and colons: `{"wheel_radius": 0.033, "wheelbase": 0.16}`, and you read a value with `config["wheelbase"]`.

This is how every robot stores its configuration. Positions are meaningless for parameters: nobody remembers that index 4 is the encoder resolution, but everybody understands `config["ticks_per_rev"]`. The keys are almost always strings, the values can be anything, including other dicts and lists.

Assigning to a key that does not exist creates it. Reading a key that does not exist raises a KeyError and stops the program, which for a missing calibration parameter is the right thing to happen at startup rather than halfway through a mission.
lessons.task: Build the robot config dict with five parameters, read three of them into local names, and print a startup line reporting the geometry.
lessons.starter:
config = {"name": "ORBITAL-1"}

print(config["name"])
lessons.solution:
config = {
    "name": "ORBITAL-1",
    "wheel_radius_m": 0.033,
    "wheelbase_m": 0.16,
    "ticks_per_rev": 20,
    "max_speed_ms": 0.45,
}

name = config["name"]
wheelbase = config["wheelbase_m"]
max_speed = config["max_speed_ms"]

print(f"{name}: wheelbase {wheelbase:.3f} m, top speed {max_speed:.2f} m/s")
print(f"keys loaded: {len(config)}")
lessons.hint: Keys go in quotes inside the square brackets: `config["wheelbase_m"]`.

lessons.title: When the Key Is Not There
lessons.goal: Read optional configuration safely with get and a default.
lessons.theory:
`config.get("ramp_s", 0.2)` returns the value if the key exists and 0.2 if it does not, without raising. That single method is the difference between a config file that must list every parameter and one where the user only writes what differs from the defaults.

Decide per parameter which behaviour you want. A missing wheel radius should crash: there is no sane default for the geometry of a machine you cannot see. A missing log level should quietly become `"INFO"`. Using `[]` for the first and `.get()` for the second is a design decision, not a style choice.

`in` tests membership: `if "ramp_s" in config:` is `True` when the key exists. Use it when you need to react to the absence itself, for example to log that a default was applied.
lessons.task: Read two required parameters with square brackets and two optional ones, `ramp_s` and `log_level`, with `get`, report which optional keys fell back to defaults, and print the effective configuration.
lessons.hint: `config.get(key, fallback)` never raises. `key not in config` tells you the fallback was used.

lessons.title: Walking the Joint Table
lessons.goal: Iterate a dict with items, keys and values.
lessons.theory:
`for key in d:` walks the keys. `for value in d.values():` walks the values. `for key, value in d.items():` gives both, and it is the one you will use most.

A six axis arm keeps its state as a dict from joint name to angle. Printing the whole state, checking every joint against its limit, or sending them all to the driver are all one `items()` loop. Since Python 3.7 dicts keep insertion order, so the joints come out base first and wrist last, which is what a human reading the log expects.

Do not add or remove keys while iterating a dict, it raises a RuntimeError. If you need to modify, iterate over `list(d.keys())` so you are walking a snapshot.
lessons.task: Walk the joint angle dict with `items()`, print each joint with its angle in degrees, and report in `worst_name` the joint that is furthest from zero.
lessons.solution:
import math

joints_rad = {"base": 0.52, "shoulder": -1.05, "elbow": 1.31, "wrist": -0.18}

worst_name = ""
worst_mag = 0.0

for name, rad in joints_rad.items():
    deg = math.degrees(rad)
    print(f"{name:9s} {rad:+.3f} rad {deg:+7.2f} deg")
    if abs(rad) > worst_mag:
        worst_mag = abs(rad)
        worst_name = name

print(f"furthest from home: {worst_name} at {math.degrees(worst_mag):.2f} deg")
lessons.hint: `for name, rad in joints_rad.items():` unpacks key and value in the loop header.

lessons.title: The State That Changes
lessons.goal: Add, update and remove keys to maintain a live robot state dict.
lessons.theory:
Dicts are mutable. `state["mode"] = "AUTO"` sets or replaces a key. `state.update(other)` merges another dict in, overwriting matching keys. `del state["fault"]` removes one, and `state.pop("fault", None)` removes it without raising if it was already gone.

This is the shape of a robot's live state: one dict updated every cycle, holding pose, battery, mode and any active fault. Behaviours read it, one place writes it. Merging a partial update from a sensor is a single `update` call.

The safe removal matters more than it looks. Clearing a fault that already cleared itself is a normal event in a control loop, and it should not be a crash. `pop` with a default is the idiom for that.
lessons.task: Maintain the state dict across three cycles: set a fault, merge a telemetry update, then clear the fault safely and print the state each time.
lessons.starter:
state = {"mode": "IDLE", "battery_v": 11.7}

print(state)
lessons.solution:
state = {"mode": "IDLE", "battery_v": 11.7}
print(f"cycle 1 {state}")

state["mode"] = "FAULT"
state["fault"] = "bumper_left"
print(f"cycle 2 {state}")

state.update({"battery_v": 11.4, "x_m": 0.35, "y_m": 0.10})
print(f"cycle 3 {state}")

cleared = state.pop("fault", None)
state["mode"] = "AUTO"
print(f"cycle 4 cleared={cleared} {state}")
print(f"second clear returns {state.pop('fault', None)}")
lessons.hint: `state.update({...})` merges several keys at once, `state.pop(key, None)` removes without raising.

lessons.title: Limits Inside Limits
lessons.goal: Nest dicts to describe per joint configuration and read them in two steps.
lessons.theory:
A value in a dict can be another dict. `limits["elbow"]["max_deg"]` reads a nested structure two levels deep, and that is exactly how a real robot description looks: one entry per joint, each holding its minimum, maximum and maximum speed.

The alternative, flat keys like `"elbow_max_deg"`, works until you need to loop over the joints. With nesting you can walk every joint and check every field with a single `items()` loop and no string surgery.

Reach two levels down and both levels can be missing. `limits.get("elbow", {}).get("max_deg", 180)` is the defensive form: a missing joint yields an empty dict, and the second `get` then falls back cleanly. It is ugly and it is what you want when parsing a config file written by a human.
lessons.task: Store per joint limits as a nested dict, then validate a set of commanded angles against them and print one verdict line per joint: accepted when the angle sits inside its envelope, REJECTED with the envelope shown when it does not.
lessons.hint: `limits.get(joint, {}).get("min_deg", -180.0)` survives both a missing joint and a missing field.

lessons.title: Counting What Went Wrong
lessons.goal: Build a histogram in a dict to count events over a run.
lessons.theory:
To count occurrences you need a dict from event to count, and one line to increment it: `counts[code] = counts.get(code, 0) + 1`. The `get` with a default of zero handles the first time you see a code, so there is no special case.

This is how you turn a log into a diagnosis. Two hundred cycles of a rover produce a stream of fault codes, and the raw stream tells you nothing. The histogram tells you that `ENCODER_STALL_LEFT` fired forty times and everything else fired twice, which points at one motor.

`sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)` orders the histogram by count. The `key` argument takes a function that extracts what to sort by, and `lambda` is a small anonymous function written inline. That is the one place a lambda genuinely earns its keep.
lessons.task: Count the fault codes from a run, then print them ordered from most to least frequent along with the total number of events.
lessons.hint: `counts.get(code, 0) + 1` is the whole counter. Sort with `key=lambda kv: kv[1]` and `reverse=True`.

lessons.title: The Set of Faults Seen
lessons.goal: Use a set for uniqueness and fast membership tests.
lessons.theory:
A **set** holds unique values with no order: `{"BUMPER_L", "IMU_SATURATED"}`, or `set()` for an empty one. Adding a value that is already there does nothing, which is precisely what you want for the collection of faults seen during a run.

Membership testing is where sets shine. `code in critical_faults` is fast no matter how large the set is, while the same test on a list walks every element. In a control loop that checks a fault against a blacklist every cycle, that difference is real.

The set operations read like the questions you actually ask: `active & critical` gives the faults that are both active and critical, `active - acknowledged` gives the ones nobody has cleared, `a | b` merges two sets. Expressing safety logic as set algebra instead of nested loops makes it short enough to review.
lessons.task: Build the set of faults seen in the run, intersect it with the critical set to decide whether to halt, and print which non critical faults remain.
lessons.starter:
events = ["ENC_STALL_L", "IMU_SATURATED", "ENC_STALL_L", "BUMPER_L"]
CRITICAL = {"ENC_STALL_L", "OVERCURRENT", "ESTOP"}

seen = set()
print(seen)
lessons.solution:
events = ["ENC_STALL_L", "IMU_SATURATED", "ENC_STALL_L", "BUMPER_L"]
CRITICAL = {"ENC_STALL_L", "OVERCURRENT", "ESTOP"}

seen = set()
for code in events:
    seen.add(code)

blocking = seen & CRITICAL
minor = seen - CRITICAL

print(f"{len(events)} events, {len(seen)} distinct")
print(f"blocking: {sorted(blocking)}")
print(f"minor:    {sorted(minor)}")

if blocking:
    print("HALT, critical fault latched")
else:
    print("run may continue")
lessons.hint: `seen.add(code)` builds the set, `seen & CRITICAL` is the intersection and `seen - CRITICAL` the difference.

lessons.title: Cutting Up a Serial Line
lessons.goal: Parse a delimited telemetry string with strip, split and float.
lessons.theory:
An MPU6050 bridged through an Arduino sends lines like `IMU,0.12,-0.03,9.81\r\n`. Your program receives text and has to turn it into numbers.

Three methods do the job. `.strip()` removes the whitespace and line endings at both ends, and forgetting it is why `float("9.81\r")` fails on Windows style line endings. `.split(",")` cuts the line into a list of pieces. `float(piece)` converts one piece to a number.

Always check the piece count before you index. A serial line can arrive truncated because the buffer filled or the robot was reset mid transmission, and `parts[3]` on a two field line raises an IndexError inside your control loop. Check `len(parts)` and the tag first, then convert.
lessons.task: Parse a list of raw serial lines: strip, split, verify the tag and field count, convert to floats and print the magnitude of the acceleration, skipping malformed lines.
lessons.solution:
import math

lines = ["IMU,0.12,-0.03,9.81\r\n", "IMU,0.05\r\n", "  IMU,-0.20,0.02,9.78  \n", "GPS,1,2,3\n"]

for raw in lines:
    parts = raw.strip().split(",")
    if len(parts) != 4 or parts[0] != "IMU":
        print(f"dropped malformed frame: {raw.strip()!r}")
        continue
    ax = float(parts[1])
    ay = float(parts[2])
    az = float(parts[3])
    mag = math.sqrt(ax * ax + ay * ay + az * az)
    print(f"ax={ax:+.2f} ay={ay:+.2f} az={az:+.2f} |a|={mag:.3f} m/s2")
lessons.hint: `raw.strip().split(",")` in one chain, then guard on `len(parts)` before touching any index.

lessons.title: Building the Command to Send
lessons.goal: Assemble an outgoing protocol string with join and formatting.
lessons.theory:
Going the other way, you have numbers and you need one line of text ending in a newline. `",".join(pieces)` glues a list of **strings** with a separator, so every number has to be formatted first.

Fix the number of decimals on the way out. A wheel speed printed as `0.30000000000000004` wastes bytes on a 115200 baud link and can overflow a fixed size buffer on the microcontroller receiving it. `f"{v:.3f}"` gives you a predictable width.

Add a checksum while you are here. Summing the character codes of the payload modulo 256 costs one line and lets the receiver discard corrupted frames, which on a long unshielded cable next to a motor driver is not paranoia, it is Tuesday.
lessons.task: Write `build_frame(left, right)` that returns a comma separated command with three decimals, an XOR checksum in hex and a trailing newline, then print the frames for three commands.
lessons.hint: Format each number into a string first, then `",".join(...)` the list of strings.

lessons.title: Opening the Calibration File
lessons.goal: Read a text file line by line using with open.
lessons.theory:
`open(path)` gives you a file object, and `with open(path) as f:` closes it automatically when the block ends, even if the code inside raises. Always use the `with` form. A robot process that leaks file handles for days eventually runs out of them and dies at the worst moment.

Iterating a file object walks it line by line, and each line still carries its trailing newline, so `.strip()` is part of the ritual. Blank lines and comment lines starting with `#` are normal in a hand edited calibration file and you skip them before parsing. The comment test is `str.startswith`, the string method that answers whether a string begins with a given prefix, so `line.startswith("#")` is the whole check.

Here you write the file first and then read it back, so the exercise runs anywhere. That round trip is also how you should test file code for real: create the input in the test, do not depend on a file that happens to be on your machine.
lessons.task: Write a small calibration file, then read it back with `with open`, skipping blanks and comments, and print every key and value you recover.
lessons.starter:
PATH = "calib.txt"

with open(PATH, "w") as f:
    f.write("# calibration\nwheel_radius_m=0.033\n")

print("written")
lessons.solution:
PATH = "calib.txt"

with open(PATH, "w") as f:
    f.write("# ORBITAL-1 calibration\n")
    f.write("wheel_radius_m=0.0331\n")
    f.write("\n")
    f.write("wheelbase_m=0.1605\n")
    f.write("ticks_per_rev=20\n")

calib = {}
with open(PATH) as f:
    for line in f:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        key, value = line.split("=", 1)
        calib[key] = value

for key, value in calib.items():
    print(f"{key:16s} = {value}")
lessons.hint: `with open(PATH) as f:` then `for line in f:`. Skip a line when it is empty or starts with `#`.

lessons.title: The Flight Recorder
lessons.goal: Append telemetry to a log file and control flushing.
lessons.theory:
The mode you pass to `open` decides everything. `"w"` truncates the file to empty before writing, `"a"` appends to what is there, `"r"` is read only and is the default. Opening a mission log with `"w"` instead of `"a"` erases yesterday's evidence, and that mistake is made once per career.

Writes are buffered. Python holds your text in memory and writes it in blocks, which is fast and means that if the robot loses power the last lines never reach the disk. `f.flush()` pushes the buffer out immediately. For telemetry at 50 Hz, flushing every line will hammer an SD card, so flush on events that matter: mode changes, faults, mission end.

`f.write()` does not add a newline for you. Every line you write ends in an explicit `\n` or the whole log becomes one enormous line.

To count what you recorded, reopen the file and call `io.IOBase.readlines`, the file object method that returns the whole file as a list of strings, one per line. `len(f.readlines())` is then the number of lines on disk.
lessons.task: Open a log in append mode, write ten timestamped telemetry lines, flush after the fault line, then reopen the file and print how many lines it holds.
lessons.starter:
LOG = "run.log"

with open(LOG, "w") as f:
    f.write("t,left,right\n")

print("log started")
lessons.solution:
LOG = "run.log"

with open(LOG, "w") as f:
    f.write("t_s,left_ms,right_ms,event\n")

with open(LOG, "a") as f:
    for i in range(10):
        t = i * 0.05
        event = "fault" if i == 6 else "ok"
        f.write(f"{t:.2f},0.300,0.250,{event}\n")
        if event == "fault":
            f.flush()

with open(LOG) as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print(f"log holds {len(lines)} lines")
print(lines[0].strip())
print(lines[-1].strip())
lessons.hint: Open once with `"w"` for the header, then with `"a"` for the rows. Every write ends in `\n`.

lessons.title: The Run in Columns
lessons.goal: Read and write CSV files with the csv module.
lessons.theory:
Splitting on commas by hand works until a field contains a comma, and then it silently corrupts your data. The `csv` module in the standard library handles quoting, escaping and line endings correctly, and it costs one import.

`csv.DictWriter` writes rows from dicts using a `fieldnames` list, `writeheader()` emits the header row, and `csv.DictWriter.writerow` emits one data row per dict. `csv.DictReader` reads them back and gives you one dict per row, keyed by the header. That symmetry means the header of your log file is also the schema of your analysis code.

Everything DictReader returns is a **string**. `float(row["left_ms"])` is not optional, and forgetting it gives you a mean computed by concatenating text, which fails loudly, or a comparison that quietly always returns the same answer.
lessons.task: Write a four column run log with `csv.DictWriter`, read it back with `csv.DictReader`, and print the mean commanded speed and the row where the fault occurred.
lessons.starter:
import csv

PATH = "run.csv"
FIELDS = ["t_s", "left_ms", "right_ms", "event"]

with open(PATH, "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=FIELDS)
    writer.writeheader()

print("csv ready")
lessons.solution:
import csv

PATH = "run.csv"
FIELDS = ["t_s", "left_ms", "right_ms", "event"]
rows = [
    {"t_s": 0.00, "left_ms": 0.30, "right_ms": 0.30, "event": "ok"},
    {"t_s": 0.05, "left_ms": 0.30, "right_ms": 0.28, "event": "ok"},
    {"t_s": 0.10, "left_ms": 0.15, "right_ms": 0.15, "event": "slow"},
    {"t_s": 0.15, "left_ms": 0.00, "right_ms": 0.00, "event": "fault"},
]

with open(PATH, "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=FIELDS)
    writer.writeheader()
    for row in rows:
        writer.writerow(row)

total = 0.0
n = 0
fault_at = None
with open(PATH, newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        total = total + float(row["left_ms"])
        n = n + 1
        if row["event"] == "fault":
            fault_at = float(row["t_s"])

print(f"{n} rows, mean left {total / n:.3f} m/s")
print(f"fault at t={fault_at:.2f} s")
lessons.hint: `csv.DictReader(f)` yields dicts of strings. Convert with `float()` before doing arithmetic.

lessons.title: Config That Survives a Reboot
lessons.goal: Save and load structured configuration with json.
lessons.theory:
JSON is the format for anything with nesting: dicts inside dicts, lists of waypoints, per joint limits. `json.dump(obj, f, indent=2)` writes it readable, `json.load(f)` reads it back into real Python objects with the right types.

Types survive the round trip, which is why JSON beats your own key equals value format the moment a value stops being a string. A float stays a float, a list of tuples comes back as a list of **lists**, and `True` comes back as `True`. That tuple to list conversion is the one asymmetry worth remembering.

Write the config to a temporary name and rename it over the real one if you can. A robot that loses power midway through rewriting its config file wakes up with a truncated file and no way to boot, and the atomic rename is the standard cure.
lessons.task: Save a nested robot config to JSON, with the waypoint list stored under a `mission` key, load it back, and prove the round trip by printing a nested value and the number of waypoints.
lessons.starter:
import json

PATH = "robot.json"
config = {"name": "ORBITAL-1"}

with open(PATH, "w") as f:
    json.dump(config, f, indent=2)

print("saved")
lessons.solution:
import json

PATH = "robot.json"
config = {
    "name": "ORBITAL-1",
    "geometry": {"wheel_radius_m": 0.0331, "wheelbase_m": 0.1605},
    "limits": {"max_speed_ms": 0.45, "max_yaw_rps": 1.8},
    "mission": [[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.8]],
    "reversed_left": False,
}

with open(PATH, "w") as f:
    json.dump(config, f, indent=2)

with open(PATH) as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print(f"wheelbase {loaded['geometry']['wheelbase_m']} m")
print(f"{len(loaded['mission'])} waypoints, first {loaded['mission'][0]}")
print(f"round trip identical: {loaded == config}")
lessons.hint: `json.dump(config, f, indent=2)` to write, `json.load(f)` to read. Keep what comes back in a variable called `loaded` so you can compare it against the original `config`, and reach nested values with two lookups.

lessons.title: Catching the Bad Frame
lessons.goal: Handle a failure with try and except instead of crashing.
lessons.theory:
`try:` runs code that might fail, `except:` catches the failure and lets the program continue. Without it, one malformed serial frame kills a robot that was otherwise fine.

Catch **specific** exceptions. `except ValueError:` catches a failed `float()` conversion. A bare `except:` catches everything including the KeyboardInterrupt you press to stop the robot, which is how people end up unable to stop their own machine. Name the exception you expect and let the ones you did not expect crash loudly, because a crash you can read beats a robot that keeps driving in an unknown state.

The exception object carries information. `except ValueError as e:` binds it to `e` so you can log what actually went wrong, which is the difference between a useful log and the word `error`.
lessons.task: Parse a list of serial frames inside a try block, catch `ValueError` and `IndexError` separately, count the good and bad frames and print the reason each bad one failed.
lessons.starter:
frames = ["IMU,0.12,-0.03,9.81", "IMU,x,0.0,9.8", "IMU,0.1"]
good = 0
bad = 0

print(good, bad)
lessons.solution:
